newsitem.title: UK: BA expects UK-US open skies talks to resume.
newsitem.headline: BA expects UK-US open skies talks to resume.

text.p: British Airways Plc said on Tuesday that it believed a breakdown in "open skies" talks between Britain and the United States was only temporary and a deal would be cut sooner or later.

The U.S. Department of Transportation said earlier that its officials had called off a meeting due to be held this week because the latest proposals from their counterparts at the British Department of Transport "did not provide the basis for discussion".
"We are sure that the delay is only temporary," a spokesman for British Airways said.

"Both sides are committed, on the right terms, to deliver an open skies agreement. It's a bold and imaginative objective and inevitably given the scale of what is being attempted some complications were inevitable," he said.

The U.S. has made any approval of BA's controversial alliance with American Airlines conditional on first getting an open skies agreement which would open up London Heathrow, Europe's busiest airport, to all U.S. carriers.
Under the current agreement dating back to 1977 only four airlines can use Heathrow for transatlantic flights -- BA, American, United Airlines and Virgin Atlantic.

According to U.S. airline sources this week's meeting was billed as an interim session focusing on technical issues but U.S. officials were then led to believe the meeting would explore possibilities for a compromise deal.

They said this was because British officials said they had constructive proposals and wanted to conduct negotiations in private, asking their counterparts not to brief their airlines on how the talks were going, as they normally do.
Britain's Department of Transport routinely declines to comment on the progress of the talks, arguing that it would be tantamount to negotiating through the media.

BA's domestic long-haul rival Virgin Atlantic said on Tuesday that it was disappointed the talks had broken down but it deplored the idea that this week's meeting might have had a hidden agenda to discuss substantive issues in secret.
"The talks this week were going to be conducted behind closed doors when we were told they were merely procedural," said Virgin's chief spokesman, Will Whitehorn.

"We have always said that negotiations affecting so many British and American consumers should be conducted in an open forum," he said. "It is our belief that all airlines and the public in general should be kept informed."
